title: How decision briefs should work
description: Four choices about the shared decision brief: its layout, how answers come back at work, where decisions are recorded, and when agents make one. This page is itself the first brief made with it.
why: You asked for one skill and template that any agent, skill or persona in Flight Deck uses for complex decisions, so every brief looks the same and nobody pays to rebuild it. It is built (`skills/decision-brief`). **This page is its first brief:** the agent wrote only a 17 KB data file, and the template drew the rest.
Four choices are left that change how it feels to use. Each is drawn the way it would look, so you can judge the design and decide at the same time.
how_to_answer: Pick an option on each decision, or Something else, and add a note if you like. Picks save to this page as you go and I read them from there. Point at an option to see it drawn. To comment on a part of the page, use Comment on this, or the page's comment mode.
recommendation: Keep the layout you see here: one page, the briefing and picture beside your call, stacked on a phone. At work, Send puts your answers in the chat box for you to send, which works today and never sends without you; a one-press version can follow. Each decision goes to the initiative's decisions register, with a short note beside the brief that links the research and the archived page. Agents make a brief when a choice has real tradeoffs and is hard to undo, visual, linked to other choices, or needed research; a simple choice stays a question card.

findings.title: Every brief was built from scratch.
findings.body: The 22 archived pages share one shape (briefing, options with consequences, a recommendation, Something else, a note, saved answers) but each carries its own styles and scripts, about 220 KB of hand-written styles between them.

findings.title: Answers were saved two ways.
findings.body: Of the 9 pages that saved answers for Claude, some wrote `pick`, `note` and `title`, others `choice`, `label` and `text`. Reading them back meant guessing.

findings.title: duo-v2's best page was data, not markup.
findings.body: The GitHub issues page held its decisions as a list and drew them with one script, with the recommendation in a paragraph and "Accept all recommendations". That is the model here.

findings.title: The picture works best beside the question.
findings.body: The duo mockups that tested best put a stage that redraws for the option you are looking at next to a Your call panel. On a phone they stack.

findings.title: At work, a page can't save for Claude.
findings.body: Flight Deck has no page database. An artifact can only keep its own view state and put text in the chat box for you to send (`omnigent.prompt`). So answers travel as text there.

decisions.label: DB-1
decisions.question: How should a brief lay out each decision?
context: Every brief uses one layout, so this choice sets how all of them read from now on. It is cheap to change later, because the layout lives in one template.
know: This page uses the first option. Narrow the window to see it stack.
Narration (a voice and captions) was the most liked in duo-v2 but needs a recording per brief, which Flight Deck can't do offline.

options.label: One page, briefing beside your call
options.consequence: Everything on one scrolling page: you see all the decisions, their order and what is answered. On a phone each card stacks, picture first. What you are looking at now.

decisions.label: DB-2
decisions.question: Inside Flight Deck at work, how do your answers reach the agent?
context: On claude.ai (pages like this one) your picks save to the page and I read them. Flight Deck at work has no page database, so the brief needs another way back. Whichever you pick, the answers end up in the brief's data file, where any agent can read them.
know: Today an artifact can only put text in the chat box (you press Send) or keep its own view state between reloads.
The app already sends some changes straight to the agent (a canvas action), but only status words. Answers carry your notes, so they would need a small change to the app.

options.label: Send puts them in the chat box; you press Send
options.consequence: One button collects every answer and note into the chat box as a short list. You see exactly what goes, and press Send. Nothing leaves without you. One extra press.

visual.caption: Your picks stay on the page across reloads; Send fills the chat box; the agent writes them to the brief and confirms in one line.

options.label: Straight to the agent, one press
options.consequence: The page sends your answers itself, the way status changes already go. One press fewer, but the app must learn to carry notes safely, and you don't see the message before it goes.

visual.caption: Like a canvas action: the app writes the message from checked values and sends it.
visual.html:

options.label: Saved to a file the agent reads when asked
options.consequence: No message at all: answers land in a file and the agent picks them up when you next say something. Quietest, but the agent doesn't know you answered until you tell it.

decisions.reason: It works today with no change to the app, it keeps the rule that nothing is sent without you, and it leaves a readable record of your answers in the conversation. One press fewer can come later.

decisions.label: DB-3
decisions.question: Where should a decision be written down once you lock it?
context: You asked for a decision note in the repo after you lock your picks, linking the research, the rationale and the archived page. The question is where that note sits, and whether the decision also goes in the initiative's decisions register (D-141, D-142), which every skill reads before asking again.
know: For this repo's own decisions nothing changes: they still get D-numbers in `docs/product/decisions.md`. The note says which numbers.
In Flight Deck an initiative's register is what stops a later skill asking you the same thing again.

options.label: The register, plus a note beside the brief
options.consequence: Each decision becomes one line in the initiative's decisions register, so every skill sees it. A short note beside the brief keeps the why, the options considered and the links. Two places, each with one job.

options.label: Only the note
options.consequence: One file per brief and nothing else. Simple, but other skills don't see the decision unless they find the note, so they may ask again.

options.label: One decisions log for the whole workspace
options.consequence: Like this repo's `decisions.md`: every decision in one numbered file. Easy to scan, but it mixes initiatives and duplicates the registers the skills already use.

visual.html:

└─ decisions.md                  D-01 … D-87, all initiatives

decisions.reason: The register is the one place skills already read before asking (D-142), and the note keeps the rationale and links without bloating it. It is what the lifecycle thread's Decide move expects, too.

decisions.label: DB-4
decisions.question: When should an agent make a brief instead of asking with a card?
context: A brief costs a few minutes and your attention; a question card costs a tap. The rule decides which one Aviator, the director and every skill reach for. It is written once, in the skill and the workspace's instructions, and other skills point to it.
know: A brief is never made for a choice the person can make in seconds, and never for work the agent can just do and undo.
Whichever you pick, you can always ask for a brief ("brief me on this") or say "just ask me".

stage.caption: How the recommended rule sorts some real asks.
stage.html:
The askWhyGets
Which of two titles for the PRD?One quick choiceCard
Cut scope or move the date for checkout?Real tradeoffs, hard to undoBrief
Which of four layouts for the status page?VisualBrief
Five open questions from the risk reviewSeveral linked decisionsBrief
Rename a field in the catalogEasy to undo; just do itNeither

options.label: A rule: real tradeoffs, plus one more sign
options.consequence: A brief when there are two or more real options with tradeoffs and the choice is hard to undo, visual, one of several linked decisions, or needed research to frame. Otherwise a card. Agents say in one line why they made a brief.

options.label: Only when you ask for one
options.consequence: Everything is a card unless you say "brief me". Fewer pages, but big choices arrive as a tap with no picture, which is what you asked us not to do.

options.label: Any choice with more than one option
options.consequence: Consistent, but small choices cost a page each, and you get a lot of pages.

decisions.reason: It matches what you have asked for so far (never decide blind on big or visual choices, tap for small ones) and it is short enough for every skill to apply the same way. It can be tuned with the routing evals later.

after: I write your answers into the brief's data file, lock them, and write the decision note with links to this page, its archived copy and the research.
Anything you change goes into the template once, so every brief after it changes too.
The decisions get D-numbers in the repo, and the archived copy of this page goes in `docs/decision-artifacts/`.
